nodes.label: GitBook Documentation Config
nodes.rationale: Publishes only ./docs/ to GitBook, with README.md as the landing page and SUMMARY.md as the navigation tree; the root README.md and IMPLEMENTATION.md are deliberately outside the published site.

nodes.label: Go CI Build and Test Workflow
nodes.rationale: Builds everything (go build ./...) but only tests ./event/..., so the examples/ programs are compile-checked and never executed in CI.
nodes.norm_label: go ci build and test workflow

nodes.label: In-Process Only Scope
nodes.rationale: Publish puts the event on a Go channel and a worker goroutine picks it up: no broker, no network hop. Stated explicitly so users do not mistake it for a replacement for Kafka, NATS or Redis Pub/Sub; the trade-off accepted is that nothing survives a process crash.

nodes.label: Shutdown Drains the Backlog
nodes.rationale: Shutdown used to cancel the context and discard buffered events; it now delivers them, waits for workers, and cancels the context last. Waits at most Config.ShutdownTimeout (5s default) and returns a TimeoutError otherwise. Consequence for users: post-publish sleeps can usually be deleted.

nodes.label: WithRecovery Reports the Panic
nodes.rationale: It used to return nil, making a panicking handler indistinguishable from a clean one. It now returns an errors.ProcessingError, so chaining with WithRetry means a panicking handler is retried. Source-compatible but behaviourally visible on upgrade.

nodes.label: Publish Returns Bool, Shutdown Returns Error
nodes.rationale: false from Publish means the event was dropped -- a full buffer or a bus already shutting down. Statement-style calls stay source-compatible, so the change is opt-in for readers of the return value.
nodes.norm_label: publish returns bool, shutdown returns error

nodes.label: Standard Error Types
nodes.rationale: Nine typed errors (Retryable, Validation, Processing, Timeout, Fatal, TypeAssertion, NoData, InvalidEvent, UnsupportedEventType) each with New<Type>Error and New<Type>Errorf. The *Errorf variants leave Message empty and put formatted text in Err, which is what lets the format string wrap a cause with %w.

nodes.label: Pre-defined Error Constants
nodes.rationale: Sentinel values (ErrNilData, ErrTypeAssertionFailed, ...) modelled on io.EOF and redis.Nil so callers can use errors.Is for common cases without constructing an error.

nodes.label: Middleware Chain Ordering Rule
nodes.rationale: Order is outermost-first, so WithRecovery goes last in the argument list: it turns a panic into an error and everything wrapped around it gets to see that error. WithRecovery is not optional insurance -- an unrecovered panic takes down the worker goroutine and with it the process.

nodes.label: Event Filtering
nodes.rationale: FilterByMetadata plus And/Or combinators wrapped in NewFilteredProcessor; benchmarked at ~30ns and zero allocations, so filtering to avoid work is nearly free.

nodes.label: Batch Processing
nodes.rationale: Recommended above 1000 events/second. Shutdown order matters: the bus feeds the batch, so drain the bus first and shut the batch down second. Without BatchConfig.OnError a failing batch is silent -- the batch is gone and nothing is told.

nodes.label: Bulk Subscription
nodes.rationale: SubscribeMultiple / UnsubscribeMultiple let one processor serve several event types, which is the shape wanted for cross-cutting concerns like audit logging and metrics.

nodes.label: Safe Type Casting with CastEventData
nodes.rationale: Three nil-checking strategies for the typed-nil trap: default fast path (untyped nils only, zero overhead), WithReflectNilCheck (reflection, catches typed nils), WithCustomNilCheck (zero-allocation caller-supplied checker for hot paths).

nodes.label: Benchmark Results and Allocation Profile
nodes.rationale: Publishing and filtering allocate nothing; subscribing allocates a little; unsubscribing deliberately allocates a fresh slice so the frequent operation stays cheap; WithTimeout is an order of magnitude more expensive than everything else.

nodes.label: WithTimeout Per-Event Goroutine Cost
nodes.rationale: It is the one middleware with a real per-event cost -- 1427 ns/op and 560 B/op -- because it starts a goroutine and a channel for every event. Filters, WithRetry on the success path, and WithLogging are just function calls.

nodes.label: Hierarchical Event Naming
nodes.rationale: domain.entity.action, e.g. auth.user.created, order.payment.completed, inventory.stock.updated.

nodes.label: Synchronise Tests on Shutdown, Not Sleep
nodes.rationale: Shutdown drains everything accepted and returns when workers are done, so the assertion is exact and there is no timing to tune. Shutdown is idempotent, so a defer alongside an explicit drain is a safety net rather than a bug.
nodes.norm_label: synchronise tests on shutdown, not sleep

nodes.label: Open/Closed Principle Motivation
nodes.rationale: The library exists because CreateUser-style functions that inline email, audit, metrics and notification calls must be modified for every new side effect. Publishing an event makes the code open for extension and closed for modification.

nodes.label: EventBus Coordinator
nodes.rationale: Holds subscriptions map, buffered eventChan, worker count, shutdownTimeout, a monotonic subscriptionSeq, ctx/cancel, RWMutex, closed flag, shutdownOnce and a WaitGroup. NewEventBus replaces any Config field left at zero or below with its default, because none of those values describes a working bus.

nodes.label: EventType Strong Typing
nodes.rationale: A named string type rather than raw strings so a typo like UserCraeted becomes a compile error and the IDE can autocomplete the constants.

nodes.label: Event Structure
nodes.rationale: Type, Timestamp, Data (any) and Metadata. NewEvent exists so Timestamp and the Metadata map are never left uninitialised; WithMetadata returns the event so construction reads as a chain. Events are treated as immutable after creation, which is what makes them safe to hand to several processors at once.

nodes.label: EventProcessor Function Type
nodes.rationale: func(ctx context.Context, event *Event) error -- a plain function rather than an interface, which is what makes middleware, filters and the batch adapter composable as ordinary function wrappers.

nodes.label: Subscription Registry
nodes.rationale: map[EventType][]*Subscription: a slice per event type because multiple processors subscribe to the same event. Unsubscribe deletes the map key when the last subscription goes, so empty keys do not leak.

nodes.label: Monotonic Subscription IDs
nodes.rationale: IDs are eventType plus an atomic per-bus counter. Deriving the ID from the current slice length reuses IDs after a removal, and since Unsubscribe removes the first matching ID that would silently remove the wrong handler.

nodes.label: Copy-on-Write Unsubscribe
nodes.rationale: Builds a new slice instead of append(s[:i], s[i+1:]...), because the latter shifts elements inside the backing array that dispatch walks after releasing the read lock -- a race the detector flags. Adding needs no such care: append writes at index len or allocates outright. Unsubscribe is the rare operation and deliberately pays so dispatch does not.

nodes.label: Non-Blocking Publish with Drop Reporting
nodes.rationale: A select with a default case drops rather than blocks, because blocking the publisher could freeze the whole application -- losing an event beats hanging the system. It returns bool because a dropped event nobody hears about is indistinguishable from a processed one, and only the caller knows whether this event deserves a retry, a log line, a metric, or a fall back to PublishSync.

nodes.label: Read Lock Guards the Send-on-Closed-Channel Race
nodes.rationale: Sending on a closed channel is a panic, not an error, and a closed-flag check followed by a send is not atomic -- the close can land in between. Publish holds the read lock across both the check and the send while Shutdown closes under the write lock, which makes them mutually exclusive.
nodes.norm_label: read lock guards the send-on-closed-channel race

nodes.label: Synchronous Publishing
nodes.rationale: Runs processors in the caller's goroutine and returns every error tagged with its subscription ID. Exists alongside async Publish so transactions, ordering-sensitive flows and tests can learn whether processors succeeded.

nodes.label: Dispatch and Error Collection
nodes.rationale: Takes the read lock only long enough to read the slice header, then runs each processor and collects errors instead of swallowing or logging them. Does not stop on the first error because processors are independent. Does not log because a library that logs on your behalf gives one hard-coded destination and no way to react -- compose WithLogging instead.

nodes.label: Worker Pool
nodes.rationale: start() launches cfg.Workers goroutines tracked on a WaitGroup, each ranging over the shared buffered channel. Sizing guidance: CPU-bound processors near the core count, I/O-bound higher.

nodes.label: Workers Range Over the Channel Instead of Selecting on ctx.Done
nodes.rationale: select picks a ready case at random, so once the context is cancelled a worker with a hundred buffered events is as likely to exit as to process the next one, and everything already accepted and acknowledged evaporates. range ends only when the channel is closed and drained, which is exactly the wanted shutdown behaviour.
nodes.norm_label: workers range over the channel instead of selecting on ctx.done

nodes.label: RWMutex for the Subscription Map
nodes.rationale: Dispatching (reads) is far more frequent than subscribing (writes), so a read-write mutex lets readers run concurrently where a plain Mutex would serialise them. Write locks are held for minimal time.

nodes.label: Shutdown Ordering: Close, Wait, Cancel Last
nodes.rationale: The order is the opposite of the intuitive one. Close the channel first under the write lock (the stop signal, and what stops a concurrent Publish panicking). Then wait, so ranging workers finish the buffer on their own. Cancel the context last, because cancelling first aborts the very events the drain exists to save. A ShutdownTimeout is needed because 'waiting for workers' and 'one processor wedged on a dead socket' look identical from here.
nodes.norm_label: shutdown ordering: close, wait, cancel last

nodes.label: Idempotent Shutdown via sync.Once
nodes.rationale: Two independent defers on one bus is an ordinary thing to write, and closing an already-closed channel panics. Later callers get the first call's stored result.

nodes.label: Middleware System
nodes.rationale: type Middleware func(EventProcessor) EventProcessor. Chosen over hooks because middlewares combine and are reusable across processors, where hooks are rigid and hard to compose.

nodes.label: WithRetry Middleware
nodes.rationale: Exponential backoff (delay *= 2) with a bounded attempt count, selecting on ctx.Done during the wait so shutdown does not leave it looping.

nodes.label: WithTimeout Middleware
nodes.rationale: Runs the processor in a goroutine and selects against a derived deadline, returning a TimeoutError wrapping context.DeadlineExceeded so both IsTimeout and errors.Is recognise it. A non-positive timeout is a no-op wrapper because context.WithTimeout(ctx, 0) is already expired. The done channel is buffered so the processor's goroutine can exit when nobody is left to receive. Bounds how long the middleware waits, not the processor -- a ctx-ignoring processor keeps running.

nodes.label: WithRecovery Middleware
nodes.rationale: Named return plus deferred recover converts a panic into a ProcessingError, keeping the panic value reachable through errors.As when it is itself an error. Returning nil made a panicking handler indistinguishable from a clean one. Belongs innermost in a Chain so the middleware wrapped around it observes the failure.

nodes.label: WithLogging Middleware
nodes.rationale: Takes the destination as a func(string) parameter rather than reaching for log itself, so it composes with the application's existing logger. The formatted line must go into a local: assigning it back to the captured msg prefix (a real past bug) grows the message without bound and races across concurrent events.

nodes.label: Middleware Chain
nodes.rationale: Applies middlewares in reverse index order so the first argument becomes the outermost wrapper. That is what makes recovery-innermost work: recovery turns the panic into an error, retry sees it and retries, logging records the outcome.

nodes.label: Filter and FilteredProcessor
nodes.rationale: type Filter func(*Event) bool wrapped by NewFilteredProcessor, which returns nil (not an error) when the filter rejects -- a skipped event is not a failure.

nodes.label: Filter Combinators And/Or/Not
nodes.rationale: And/Or/Not plus FilterByMetadata and FilterByMetadataExists compose arbitrary predicates out of one-line primitives, avoiding a query language.

nodes.label: Batch Processor
nodes.rationale: Buffers events under a mutex and flushes on size or on a ticker. flush copies the buffer so the lock is not held during processing, and tracks the processing goroutine on flushWg. BatchSize <= 0 clamps to 100, because len(buffer) >= 0 is true after every Add and a zero batch size would flush a batch of one per event -- the opposite of batching. Errors go to the caller's BatchErrorHandler because retry, dead-lettering and metrics are the caller's decisions.

nodes.label: FlushPeriod Ticker Guard
nodes.rationale: time.NewTicker panics on a non-positive interval, and FlushPeriod of zero is the documented way to ask for size-only batching, so it took the process down shortly after construction. Not starting the goroutine at all is what size-only should have meant. A separate stop channel rather than ctx.Done is used because the ticker must stop before the final flush while the context stays live through it.

nodes.label: Batch Shutdown Flush Ordering
nodes.rationale: Close stop, wait for the periodic goroutine, flush the remainder, wait on flushWg, cancel last. Waiting on flushWg matters because flush hands the batch to a goroutine -- without it Shutdown returns mid-write and the process can exit before the batch lands. Cancelling last matters because the final batch runs under bp.ctx, so cancelling first fails every context-aware write in it. sync.Once because a second Shutdown would close an already-closed channel.

nodes.label: Global Event Bus Singleton
nodes.rationale: GetGlobalBus and InitGlobalBus share one sync.Once, so InitGlobalBus must run before anything reaches for GetGlobalBus or the defaults win and the custom config is silently ignored. There are deliberately no package-level Publish/Subscribe shortcuts, so every call site shows that a process-wide singleton is involved.

nodes.label: any for Event Data Instead of Generics
nodes.rationale: Generics would force EventBus itself to be generic, which gets messy when one bus carries several event types. The accepted cost is no compile-time type safety on Data -- callers must type-assert.
nodes.norm_label: any for event data instead of generics

nodes.label: Functional Options for Nil Checking
nodes.rationale: An interface holding a typed nil is not equal to nil, and detecting that needs reflection, which is slow in hot paths. Rather than force reflection on everyone or ignore the problem, CastEventData defaults to the fast untyped-nil check and offers WithReflectNilCheck and WithCustomNilCheck as opt-ins, leaving the performance/safety trade-off with the caller.

nodes.label: Graceful Degradation Philosophy
nodes.rationale: A failed processor must not prevent the others from running, and event drops under high load are preferred to system overload, so one faulty processor or event cannot bring down the event system.

nodes.label: Tightly Coupled Side Effects Problem
nodes.rationale: A CreateUser that also sends email, writes an audit record, increments metrics and notifies an admin must be edited for every new side effect, violating the Open/Closed Principle.

nodes.label: Event-Driven Solution
nodes.rationale: CreateUser publishes one event and knows nothing about the reactions; adding SMS means subscribing a new processor and never touching the original function.

nodes.label: GitBook Navigation Summary
nodes.rationale: Three-section site tree (Introduction, Examples, Implementation Guide) naming docs/implementation/{overview,api,architecture}.md and five docs/examples pages that are separate files from the repo-root README.md, IMPLEMENTATION.md and examples/ directory.

nodes.label: Global Bus Singleton Recommendation
nodes.rationale: The guide recommends InitGlobalBus in main and bus.GetGlobalBus() elsewhere, so cross-package publishers need no wiring to reach the same bus.

nodes.label: Config Zero-Value Fallback
nodes.rationale: Every field falls back to its default at zero or below (10 workers, buffer 1000, 5s timeout). Out-of-range values are replaced rather than honoured: zero workers accepts events and never processes them, and a zero buffer makes the channel unbuffered, turning Publish's non-blocking send into a drop whenever no worker is free.

nodes.label: In-Process Scope and Crash Loss
nodes.rationale: No broker, no network hop, no delivery to other processes. Shutdown drains what has been accepted, but events still in the buffer when the process dies are gone -- nothing survives a crash.

nodes.label: Auth Service Example
nodes.rationale: Demonstrates event fan-out (several handlers on one event), middleware composition of retry/timeout/recovery, metadata for request correlation, and security monitoring.

nodes.label: E-commerce Example
nodes.rationale: Demonstrates batch email notification, conditional analytics for high-value orders via filters, async inventory updates and a payment pipeline.

nodes.label: Microservices Communication Example
nodes.rationale: Demonstrates cross-service decoupling over one shared in-process bus, event chaining where a service's handler publishes what another consumes, and self-registering handlers.

nodes.label: Error Handling Example
nodes.rationale: Shows conditional handling via IsRetryable/IsValidation and custom middleware that branches on error type, composed with retry and timeout.

nodes.label: Type Assertion Example
nodes.rationale: TypeAssertionError used as a redis.Nil-style sentinel for type mismatches on event.Data.

nodes.label: Event Naming Conventions
nodes.rationale: Hierarchical domain.entity.action, past tense, specific over generic, no abbreviations -- so that event names group naturally and read as facts that already happened.

nodes.label: Middleware Composition Pattern
nodes.rationale: Logging, retry, timeout, recovery chained in that order: the first is outermost, so WithRecovery last means retry retries the converted panic and logging records it. Put it first and it catches the panic only after it has unwound past them.

nodes.label: Circular Event Dependencies Pitfall
nodes.rationale: Handler A publishing B while B publishes A loops forever. Design event flow as a DAG and use metadata to track origin or recursion depth.

nodes.label: Configuration Tuning by Event Volume
nodes.rationale: Concrete Workers/BufferSize triples for low (<100/s), medium (100-1000/s) and high (>1000/s) volume, with dropped events as the signal to raise the buffer.

nodes.label: Forgetting Shutdown Pitfall
nodes.rationale: Without a deferred Shutdown, everything still in the buffer at process exit is lost. When a batch is involved the defer must drain the bus first and shut the batch down second, since deferring both in one block runs them the wrong way round and the batch refuses the tail of the backlog.

nodes.label: Synchronise Integration Tests on Shutdown
nodes.rationale: Shutdown drains everything accepted and returns once workers are done, so a test that shuts the bus down before asserting sees every published event -- no sleep to tune and nothing to go flaky under load. PublishSync is the alternative when the test also wants the handler errors.

nodes.label: WaitForEvent Polling Helper
nodes.rationale: Deadline-bounded condition polling, explicitly demoted: for a bus you own, draining with Shutdown is simpler and exact -- reach for polling only when something outside the bus has to settle too.

nodes.label: Mock Dependency Processor Testing
nodes.rationale: Because a processor is a plain function, a processor factory taking an injected collaborator (MockEmailSender) can be unit-tested with no bus at all.

nodes.label: Table-Driven Processor Tests
nodes.rationale: One table covering valid data, nil data and wrong-typed data -- the three failure modes an any-typed Data field produces.

nodes.label: Example Structure Convention
nodes.rationale: Every example is self-contained and runnable with `go run main.go`, and must demonstrate a real-world use case, best practices, integration of multiple Gossip features, testing patterns, and performance considerations. Self-containment is what lets a reader copy one example without dragging in the rest of the repo.

nodes.label: AuthService
nodes.rationale: The service holds only a bus reference and publishes events; it deliberately knows nothing about email, audit logging, or metrics. Adding SMS notification later means adding a processor, not editing AuthService.

nodes.label: AuthService.RegisterUser
nodes.rationale: Checks the bool returned by Publish and converts a rejection into a ProcessingError, because an audit-relevant registration event silently dropped by a full buffer or a shutting-down bus is indistinguishable from one that was processed.

nodes.label: Event Fan-out
nodes.rationale: One event, many handlers: registration triggers email, audit, and metrics independently. This is what buys scalability -- new processors attach to an existing event without touching the publisher.

nodes.label: Middleware Composition for Robust Processors
nodes.rationale: Chain(WithLogging, WithTimeout, WithRecovery) wraps a plain processor so cross-cutting concerns stay out of business logic and a single faulty handler cannot hang or crash the worker.

nodes.label: Bulk Subscription via SubscribeMultiple
nodes.rationale: A single processor with a type switch registered against a slice of related event types, rather than N near-identical Subscribe calls. Keeps the security-audit policy in one place.

nodes.label: Hierarchical Event Naming
nodes.rationale: Names like `auth.user.registered` encode domain, entity, and action, so event types sort and group meaningfully and cross-service collisions are unlikely.

nodes.label: Metadata for Request Tracking
nodes.rationale: Request IDs, session IDs, source and version go in Metadata rather than the payload struct, so contextual data can be added without changing the event data type.

nodes.label: batchEmailProcessor
nodes.rationale: Sends order confirmations in groups of ten (or every five seconds) instead of one email per event, because per-event overhead dominates at high volume.

nodes.label: Batch Processing for High-Volume Events
nodes.rationale: Grouping events amortises the fixed cost of an operation (an SMTP handshake, a database round-trip) across many events. Recommended above roughly 1000 events/second.

nodes.label: Conditional Processing via Event Filtering
nodes.rationale: A filter in front of the analytics processor keeps the subscription but skips work for orders under $100, so the cost of irrelevant events is a predicate call rather than a full processor run.

nodes.label: Bus-Before-Batch Shutdown Ordering
nodes.rationale: The bus feeds the batch, so the bus must drain first. Two separate defers would run in the opposite (LIFO) order and the already-shut-down batch would refuse the tail of the backlog -- hence a single defer func with the two Shutdown calls written in the required order.

nodes.label: emailNotificationProcessor (typed errors)
nodes.rationale: Returns a different typed error for each failure mode -- TypeAssertionError, NoDataError, ValidationError, RetryableError -- so downstream middleware can decide per-type whether to retry, alert, or drop.

nodes.label: WithErrorHandling (custom middleware)
nodes.rationale: Shows that Middleware is just func(EventProcessor) EventProcessor: a user can add error-type-aware behaviour without the library growing an error-handling hook.

nodes.label: Conditional Error Handling by Error Type
nodes.rationale: A type switch over IsRetryable/IsValidation/IsTimeout/IsFatal/IsProcessing lets one handler give each failure mode the response it deserves -- retry, alert developers, adjust timeouts, trip a circuit breaker -- instead of logging everything at the same severity. errors.Is against the pre-defined constants is the alternative spelling.
nodes.norm_label: conditional error handling by error type

nodes.label: Typed Errors Compose With Retry and Timeout Middleware
nodes.rationale: Because retry middleware inspects error types, marking a transient failure RetryableError is enough to get it retried; nothing has to be configured per-processor.
nodes.norm_label: typed errors compose with retry and timeout middleware

nodes.label: Self-Registering Service Handlers
nodes.rationale: Each service's constructor calls its own registerProcessors, so main() only constructs services and never carries a central wiring block that must be edited whenever a service changes what it listens to.

nodes.label: Event Chaining Across Services
nodes.rationale: A handler publishes its own event (EmailService emits email_service.email.sent while handling user_service.user.created), producing workflows nobody wrote a coordinator for.

nodes.label: Shared Event Bus Across Services
nodes.rationale: One bus instance passed to every service constructor is what lets services address each other without holding references to each other.

nodes.label: In-Process Bus, Not a Message Broker
nodes.rationale: The 'microservices' here are packages in one binary: no network hop, no cross-process delivery, nothing to run alongside the example. Gossip is a way to structure a single application around events, not a broker -- stated explicitly so readers do not deploy it as one.
nodes.norm_label: in-process bus, not a message broker

nodes.label: Per-Subscription Error Isolation
nodes.rationale: A failure in one service's processor does not stop the others: dispatch collects errors per subscription rather than aborting the dispatch, so one broken consumer cannot starve the rest.

nodes.label: FastUserDataNilChecker
nodes.rationale: A hand-written zero-allocation, reflection-free nil check for one concrete type, passed via WithCustomNilCheck to avoid the reflection cost of WithReflectNilCheck in hot paths.

nodes.label: Safe Type Assertion Over Panicking
nodes.rationale: Because Event.Data is `any`, a bare assertion panics on a mismatched payload and takes the worker goroutine with it. The comma-ok form returning a TypeAssertionError -- explicitly modelled on the redis.Nil sentinel pattern -- turns a crash into a value the caller can branch on.

nodes.label: EventBus (overview)
nodes.rationale: Owns the subscription registry, the buffered event channel, and the worker pool. Everything is in-process: Publish puts the event on a Go channel and a worker goroutine picks it up; there is no transport abstraction and no network hop.

nodes.label: EventType
nodes.rationale: A named string type rather than raw strings, so a typo like `user.craeted` is a compile error instead of a subscription that silently never fires, and IDEs can autocomplete the constants.

nodes.label: Event.WithMetadata
nodes.rationale: Lazily creates the Metadata map when it is nil, because an Event built as a struct literal -- what test fixtures and decoders produce -- carries a nil map and assigning into that panics. Returning the receiver enables fluent chaining.

nodes.label: Dispatch Without Holding the Lock
nodes.rationale: dispatch takes the read lock only long enough to read the slice header, then iterates with the lock released, so one slow processor cannot block every subscription change on the bus. The cost is moved to the write side: Unsubscribe must build a new slice, while Subscribe can append normally because an append is invisible to a reader holding the old, shorter length.

nodes.label: Why Subscription IDs Must Be Unique
nodes.rationale: IDs allow precise unsubscription without the caller remembering both event type and processor function. The ID is `<event type>-<counter>` with a per-bus monotonic counter: Unsubscribe removes the first match, so two subscriptions sharing an ID would mean removing one silently removes the other. Anything derived from slice length has the same defect -- remove one and the next subscriber is reissued that ID.
nodes.norm_label: why subscription ids must be unique

nodes.label: Why Two Publish Methods
nodes.rationale: Async Publish for performance-critical paths where the caller does not need processor outcomes; PublishSync for callers that must know whether processors failed or must complete before continuing (transactions, tests, ordering).

nodes.label: Why `any` for Event Data
nodes.rationale: Maximum payload flexibility and Go-version compatibility without forcing every event to implement an interface. Generics were rejected because making Event[T] generic forces EventBus to be generic too, which breaks down as soon as one bus carries multiple event types. The accepted cost is that processors must type-assert.

nodes.label: Buffered Channel and Drop-On-Full
nodes.rationale: The buffer decouples publishers from processors and absorbs bursts. When it fills, events are dropped rather than blocking the publisher, because blocking would freeze the whole app -- and Publish returns false so the caller decides what the drop is worth: a retry, a log line, a metric, or a fall back to PublishSync.

nodes.label: Out-of-Range Config Values Are Replaced
nodes.rationale: Zero or negative fields fall back to 10 workers, a 1000-event buffer, and a 5s shutdown timeout, because none of the out-of-range values describes a usable bus: zero workers accepts events and never processes them, and a zero buffer makes the channel unbuffered, turning Publish's non-blocking send into a drop unless a worker happens to be parked on the receive.

nodes.label: Graceful Degradation, Except for Panics
nodes.rationale: Failed processors do not prevent others from running and drops are reported rather than hidden. Panics are the deliberate exception: a panicking processor takes down the worker and the process, because silently swallowing a panic is how a broken handler stays broken. Opt in to recovery with middleware.WithRecovery(), which converts the panic into a ProcessingError.

nodes.label: EventBus.Unsubscribe
nodes.rationale: O(n) scan across all subscription lists, accepted because unsubscription is infrequent. Deletes the map key entirely when the last subscriber for a type goes, so empty keys do not leak.

nodes.label: InitGlobalBus
nodes.rationale: Shares the same sync.Once as GetGlobalBus, so it must run before anything reaches for the bus or the defaults win and the custom config is silently ignored. Call it early in main(). There are deliberately no package-level Publish/Subscribe shortcuts, so every call site shows that a process-wide singleton is involved.

nodes.label: Copy-on-Write Removal, Plain Append Addition
nodes.rationale: The obvious `append(subs[:i], subs[i+1:]...)` shifts elements down inside the backing array an in-flight dispatch is reading -- a data race the detector flags -- so removal allocates a fresh slice. Addition needs no copy: a plain append either writes at index len, invisible to a reader holding the old length, or reallocates outright. Making Subscribe copy-on-write for symmetry made every subscription an O(n) copy and took BenchmarkEventBus_Subscribe from ~355ns/op to ~183us/op.

nodes.label: Read Lock Held Across the Closed-Check and the Send
nodes.rationale: Sending on a channel closed by Shutdown is a panic, not an error, and checking a flag then sending leaves a window for the close to land between the two. Shutdown takes the write lock before closing, so holding the read lock across both check and send is what makes them mutually exclusive -- without it a request goroutine publishing at the moment of shutdown takes the process down.
nodes.norm_label: read lock held across the closed-check and the send

nodes.label: Rejecting nil Events at Publish
nodes.rationale: A nil event used to reach dispatch and nil-dereference on event.Type between the RLock and RUnlock, leaving the subscription lock held; the next Subscribe or Shutdown deadlocked behind it and the bus wedged far from the code that published nil.

nodes.label: Shutdown Ordering: Close, Wait, Cancel Last
nodes.rationale: Closing eventChan under the write lock is the stop signal and the thing that keeps a concurrent Publish from panicking. Waiting lets ranging workers finish the buffer. Cancelling the processor context is the last step, deliberately: cancelling it first would abort the very events the drain exists to save, failing every context-aware DB write and HTTP call inside them. sync.Once makes it idempotent, because two independent defers on one bus is ordinary and closing a closed channel panics; the timeout exists because 'workers still draining' and 'one processor wedged on a dead socket' look identical from here.
nodes.norm_label: shutdown ordering: close, wait, cancel last

nodes.label: Workers Range Over the Channel Instead of Selecting on ctx.Done
nodes.rationale: select picks a ready case at random, so a worker holding a hundred buffered events would be as likely to exit as to process the next one once the context was cancelled -- everything the bus had accepted and acknowledged would evaporate. A range ends only when the channel is closed and drained, which is exactly the shutdown behaviour wanted.
nodes.norm_label: workers range over the channel instead of selecting on ctx.done

nodes.label: Serial Dispatch Inside the Worker
nodes.rationale: Processors run in the calling goroutine rather than one goroutine each: concurrency across events is the worker pool's job and is bounded at Workers, whereas a goroutine per processor per event fans out unboundedly under a burst with nothing throttling it.

nodes.label: Dispatch Returns Errors Instead of Logging Them
nodes.rationale: A library that logs on your behalf gives one hard-coded destination and no way to react. PublishSync hands the errors back tagged with the subscription that produced them; a processor that wants logging composes middleware.WithLogging with a destination of its choice. A worker discards the slice.
nodes.norm_label: dispatch returns errors instead of logging them

nodes.label: RWMutex Over Mutex for the Subscription Map
nodes.rationale: Reads (dispatching) massively outnumber writes (subscribing), and RWMutex lets readers proceed concurrently where a plain Mutex would serialise every dispatch. Write locks are held only for the duration of a map mutation.
nodes.norm_label: rwmutex over mutex for the subscription map

nodes.label: Async Publishing By Default
nodes.rationale: A synchronous Publish would block the caller until every processor finished -- a five-second welcome email inside an API handler. The cost is that the publisher learns neither whether processing worked nor, on a full buffer, whether it started; the bool return covers the second half and PublishSync the first.

nodes.label: Events Treated as Immutable After Creation
nodes.rationale: Since one event pointer is handed to every subscriber concurrently across workers, not mutating it after creation is what keeps processors from racing on event data -- and avoids per-subscriber copying overhead.
nodes.norm_label: events treated as immutable after creation

nodes.label: Worker Pool Sizing Guidance
nodes.rationale: CPU-bound processors want roughly one worker per core; I/O-bound processors want more so others run while one waits; mixed workloads have to be measured.

nodes.label: WithRetry
nodes.rationale: Runs the initial attempt plus maxRetries retries, so 0 means a single attempt and a negative value is clamped to 0 -- the count is retries, not total attempts. Delay doubles after each failure.

nodes.label: WithTimeout
nodes.rationale: Reports an expired deadline as a TimeoutError wrapping context.DeadlineExceeded so both goserr.IsTimeout and errors.Is recognise it, while a cancelled parent context passes through unchanged because cancellation is not a timeout. The deadline bounds how long the middleware waits, not the processor: one that ignores ctx keeps running in its own goroutine after the timeout is reported -- which is also why this is the one middleware with real per-event overhead.

nodes.label: WithRecovery
nodes.rationale: Converts a panic into a ProcessingError (keeping an error panic value reachable through errors.As) so it does not crash the worker goroutine. Must be innermost in a Chain -- last in the argument list -- or the surrounding middleware never sees the failure, because an outer WithRecovery catches the panic only after it has unwound past them.

nodes.label: WithLogging
nodes.rationale: Takes the log destination as a func(string) parameter rather than writing to a package logger, so the library never picks the caller's logging backend.

nodes.label: Chain
nodes.rationale: Applies middlewares in reverse order (last to first), so the argument list reads outermost-to-innermost and the innermost entry is closest to the processor.

nodes.label: NewFilteredProcessor
nodes.rationale: Degrades safely on nil inputs: a nil processor yields a no-op, and a nil filter means 'no condition' so the processor runs for every event.

nodes.label: BatchConfig
nodes.rationale: A non-positive BatchSize falls back to 100; a non-positive FlushPeriod disables time-based flushing entirely, leaving Add, Flush and Shutdown as the only triggers; leaving OnError nil discards processor errors -- so the zero value is a silent batch, not a broken one.

nodes.label: Batch.Add
nodes.rationale: Returns false once the batch is shut down: nothing is left to flush the buffer, so accepting the event would only lose it more quietly.

nodes.label: Batch.Flush
nodes.rationale: Runs the processor in its own goroutine, so it returns once the buffer has been handed off, not once the batch has been written.

nodes.label: Batch.AsEventProcessor
nodes.rationale: Adapts a Batch to the EventProcessor signature so a batch can be subscribed like any processor, and returns an error after shutdown so the bus learns the event went nowhere.

nodes.label: Batch.Shutdown
nodes.rationale: Blocks until the final batch has actually been processed and only then cancels the processor context, so the last batch runs under a live one -- mirroring the bus's cancel-last ordering. A BatchProcessor that never returns will hold up shutdown. Idempotent.

nodes.label: utils.CastEventData
nodes.rationale: A generic safe cast that folds three failure modes -- nil event, failed assertion, nil data -- into typed errors, so processors stop hand-rolling comma-ok blocks. Nil-checking strategy is an option because reflection is the safe default answer to typed nils and the wrong answer in a hot path; the default is WithNoNilCheck (fastest).

nodes.label: Error Checking Functions (IsRetryable, IsFatal, IsValidation, IsTypeAssertion, IsNoData)
nodes.norm_label: error checking functions (isretryable, isfatal, isvalidation, istypeassertion, isnodata)

nodes.label: New<Type>Errorf Wrapping Constructors
nodes.rationale: The formatted variants put the text in the Err field, so the format string may use %w to wrap a cause -- errors.Is finds the cause and IsRetryable still recognises the category, giving one error that answers both questions.

nodes.label: Performance Recommendations
nodes.rationale: Tune Workers and BufferSize to the workload since events never leave the binary; batch above ~1000 events/second; filtering is near-free; middleware overhead is negligible except WithTimeout, which starts a goroutine per event.
